set.hook: Éric Canino's two-star terrace at La Réserve Ramatuelle: Guérard-school cooking, olive oil not butter.
set.why: Canino learned from Michel Guérard, who turned lightness into a haute-cuisine idea at Eugénie-les-Bains, and he has run this kitchen at Michel Reybier's La Réserve for more than fifteen years. The second star came in January 2020 and still holds. The 2026 season ran from 1 May to 11 October, every day, so the room on the Quessine hill is dark now; the vegetable menu goes from first bite to dessert without meat or fish.

set.hook: The one-star table of a Gigaro wine estate, set menus cooked from its own organic kitchen garden.

set.hook: The terrace restaurant of Starck's Gigaro wellness hotel: sun-led Mediterranean plates, lamb to share.
set.why: Vincent Maillard has cooked at Lily of the Valley since it opened on the Colline Saint-Michel in 2019, after Guy Savoy, Alain Ducasse's Louis XV with Franck Cerutti, and the Byblos. Gault&Millau's 2026 review calls it a place for insiders away from the Ramatuelle crowds, and notes a cellar long on champagne and rosé.

set.hook: Owner-run fish and Provençal table on Cavalaire's Nouveau Port, built around the grand aïoli.

set.hook: Lunch-only garden café inside the Domaine du Rayol, open all year to garden visitors.
set.why: Tom Ortin, the chef, came here from the Park Hyatt Vendôme in Paris, where he cooked beside Jean-François Rouquette. At the Domaine du Rayol he works from the garden and from local growers, with a lot of vegetables on the plate, and everything including the desserts is made on site. In November 2025 the winter card opened with a velouté of winter vegetables, and in mid-October 2026 the Domaine ran a weekend of wine paired with the food.

set.hook: Village hotel-restaurant on Gassin's rampart, in the MICHELIN selection; its 2026 season ended 11 October.
set.why: MICHELIN describes the chef as a veteran and a local lad whose grandmother lived in the village, and the house runs on the Barri, the old walk around Gassin's walls, with seven rooms and a village bar alongside. set.hook: Mouret family table in the Gassin vineyards, terrace facing Minuty and the sea; 2026 season ended 4 October.
set.why: Two generations of the Mouret family have run this farmhouse table on the slope below Gassin, and the wide terrace faces the Minuty vineyard with the Gulf of Saint-Tropez beyond. It takes bookings by telephone only, and from June to early October the tourist office warns it is full several days ahead. The cooking is southern home food scented with the hill's thyme and rosemary, fish soup and bourride among the classics.

set.hook: Cavalaire's fishermen sell the morning's catch on Quai Marc Pajot from about 10:00, weather allowing.
set.why: Cavalaire's small boats still sell part of their catch themselves, on the quay where they tie up, rather than sending all of it to auction. The town's own page says the meeting time follows the boats and the weather, from about ten, and that the fishermen hand out recipes with the fish: bream, red mullet, girelles, rockfish for the soup, a langouste on a good day. The coast's fishermen have judged their own sea since the Middle Ages; the fold at the top tells it.

set.hook: Cavalaire's year-round Provençal market, every Wednesday morning on Place Jean Moulin, 08:30–13:00.
set.why: Every Wednesday of the year the stalls go up on Place Jean Moulin, a few streets back from the port: olives, tapenade and anchoïade, pissaladière and pan bagnat to eat on the way, honey from the Maures, and the rosé of the Golfe de Saint-Tropez. In winter it is the town's own market, after the summer crowd has gone, and the one morning to stock a galley with Provençal pantry food without driving to Saint-Tropez.
